report:
Conclusion — specific, supported difference:
Model B (B minus A points toward these tokens) has a stronger “headline / newsy / sensational” initialization at the start of a sequence than Model A. In other words, B is more biased toward beginning continuations with headline-style words and dramatic/descriptive adjectives/nouns.

Why I conclude this
- The L2 difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at the earliest token position (pos0) across many middle-to-late layers (huge peaks at layers 23–25, and elevated mass from ~13 onward). That indicates the checkpoints mainly differ in how they initialize the next-token distribution at the start of a prompt.
- The logit-lens top tokens that the difference vector points toward (i.e., tokens that B is more likely to favor than A) are heavily biased toward headline-y vocabulary: “tragic”, “tragedy”, “iconic”, “vivid”, “colorful”, “loud”, “moments”, “timeless”, “headlines”, “coming/Coming”, “blitz”, “refused”, “victims”, “refugees”, “worst”, etc. Those tokens form a coherent stylistic/domain cluster (news/headline, dramatic descriptors).
- Lower-layer cells showed some product/retail tokens like “ Sale”, “rock”, “cocktail”, but these are weaker and appear at shallower layers; the dominant, high-norm signals in late layers point to the headline/sensational cluster.

Caveats
- The evidence shows a style/domain difference (tendency toward headline/sensational openings) but does not pin down a specific training objective or dataset cause (e.g., more news/headline data, reinforcement toward engagement, etc.). I don’t claim a precise training intervention — only the interpretable difference above.
- Patchscope readouts were not available in the evidence, so the conclusion rests on the layer/position norms and the logit-lens token directions.
